body: The space heater takes its time coming up orange. The colored lights are still strung along the pegboard, one more week of them, so the garage looks like a bar that closes Wednesday, and the Stroh’s fridge hums against the back wall with its door shut. Over the bench the 1964 program hangs in its freezer bag. Through the side door, thin and far off, a marching band in Pasadena. Jack sits down on the duct-taped chair with the RAZR open on his knee.

All week it has been her calling: a whisper on the back steps at midnight, the register and the ice machine, the river at dawn. He hasn’t dialed once. Tonight he does, because at his midnight he answered somebody else first, on purpose, and an hour later the clock turned over in his hand with her name on it, and he has been hearing it turn ever since.
She picks up already talking to somebody else. “Hold on. Hold on — Mama, it’s — *hold on*.” A door, and the house on her end drops by half. “You called *me*.”
“I called you.”

“Jack Costigan called me on the telephone. On purpose. Mémère, write down the date.” Behind her an old woman says something in French that doesn’t sound like anybody writing anything down. “She says it’s the first. She says she’ll remember it without a pencil.”

body.text: “You answered my midnight in the morning. I’ll allow it. Once.”
“The Gulf is still saluting your daddy. Mémère wants to know was anybody hurt.” “Tell her I’m sitting at the scene,” Jack says.
“Happy New Year, Jack. Again.”
“Happy New Year, Jack.”

body: It’s ten after five on Dupre Street, and she gives it to him in pieces. The black-eyed peas and the cabbage have been on the stove since noon. Every light in the house is still on from last night. Her daddy is in the den with the Sugar Bowl pregame, three hours early, to be sure of his chair. “Sweeping is forbidden till tomorrow. Mama’s walking around the kitchen with her hands behind her back so she won’t pick up the broom.”

Four minutes of nothing. Whether a lentil is a vegetable — “It’s a *legume*, Jack. Don’t you call my peas’ cousin a vegetable on New Year’s Day” — and whether Ohio State can keep it up, and whether Mémère, who has been told twice, will ever accept that there is a state called Oregon. Somebody wants her in the kitchen, two somebodies, and there are plates to carry.
“Call me back when y’all win.”
“And if we lose?”
“Then don’t,” Lena says, and the kitchen on Dupre Street comes up loud around her — pans, her mother, a radio — and then it’s the garage again, the heater, the band through the door.

At twenty past eight it’s over: Ohio State 26, Oregon 17, and everybody in Pasadena in their shirtsleeves going home happy. Frank turns the set off with the remote, lays the remote on the arm of his chair, and gives the whole review.
“Pryor.”
In the window chair Nonna wakes with her spoon still upright in her fist and wants to know who won. Rosie gets up off the rug and goes and shows her, in coins.

The kitchen has gone to its late shape: the supper dishes standing in the rack, the light over the stove, the window over the sink black with the yard in it. Gina is at the table with a magazine she turns a page of every few minutes without reading. Rosie is under the table in her nightgown with the blue crab, because it’s break and nobody has the strength. From the front room comes the late bowl game, two schools Frank has no feelings about, and Frank having them anyway. Jack has a glass of milk and *The Moviegoer* shut by his elbow, finished.
At twenty to ten the wall phone by the pantry rings, which on Glenwood Avenue at that hour means somebody died or somebody’s drunk.
Ma gets it with the dish towel over her shoulder. “Costigan’s.”
“Yes, this is she.” And Jack watches his mother’s face go from the face she answers the phone with to another one altogether. “*Lena.*”
Gina’s magazine goes down flat on the table.
After that it’s ten minutes of his mother’s half. He gets no more than that, and he gets all of it.
“I know, honey. I know. He told us everything. Godmother — that’s a big job. When? … Tomorrow. During the *game*? Well. That’s the South, I guess.”

She turns to the window over the sink to have the rest. “The — the *coffee*?” Her eyes come across the kitchen and land on Jack. “*That* was you. Honey, it was very good coffee. He told me *a friend*.” She listens. “Well, that’s what he said.”
“The book, yes. You *wrote* in it. I didn’t read it. I saw.”
“Him? He eats standing up. I don’t know where he gets it. His father sits.” And she laughs at the window, at something on the other end Jack will never get to hear.
From the front room, over the game: “*La suora?*”

Ma, with the receiver against her chest: “*Sì, Ma.*” Nothing else comes from the chair. Across the table Gina is mouthing things at him, enormous, a word at a time, none of which he is going to dignify.

Rosie comes out from under the table and stands at Ma’s hip until she can’t be ignored, and gets the phone in both hands. “Hi. This is Rosie.” She listens with her face turned up. “You’re welcome.” And, because a godmother ought to know: “I got a crab for Christmas. *Callinectes sapidus.*” She listens again, nods at the phone, and hands it back up. “She says that means beautiful swimmer,” she tells the kitchen, and goes back under the table.
Ma puts the receiver to her collarbone and looks at her son.
“She called *information*.”
Jack puts down his milk.
“She wants you.” Ma holds it out to him and doesn’t let go of it yet. “I don’t know why.”

The cord is the long one, the one that reaches the stove and the sink and, with a pull, the pantry, and it has been stretched that way so many times it hangs in a loop when nobody’s using it. He takes it into the pantry and pulls the door to on it, and the cord keeps the door an inch open. In here it’s the canned tomatoes, a shelf of them, and Nonna’s jars of peppers in oil with the dates on masking tape, and the bulb on its chain. He pulls the chain. Out in the kitchen Gina’s chair scrapes, and her socks go off toward the stairs.
There’s a click on the line. Upstairs, an extension coming off its hook.
“G,” he says.
Click.
“Hey,” he says, to the tomatoes.

“Hey yourself. I’m in my old room. On my old bed, under a poster of a horse I don’t remember ever wanting. Mama keeps it like a shrine: my debate trophies, my First Communion crucifix, a picture of me at the state finals in a blazer with shoulders like a linebacker. It’s a museum of a very loud child.” Something on her end chirps, a little electronic cricket. “That’s Mama’s cordless. It does that.” From somewhere down the hall in her house, music with a lot of bass in it, and then somebody making it stop.
“You called my *house*.”
“I wanted to hear your house.”
“And?”
“Your mama answers like she’s going to bill somebody.” The cricket. “I liked her. I liked her a lot. She asked me did I eat.”
“What’d you tell her?”

“The truth. Red beans at noon and a praline at four, and something green tomorrow, I promise. She said that’s what you say too.” Down the hall the bass comes back on, lower. “Now tell me where you are.”

So he tells her. The pantry: a shelf of Hunt’s, Nonna’s peppers in oil with the year on masking tape, a box of Christmas candles nobody lit, the bulb on its chain. The kitchen through the inch of door, the stove light, the refrigerator going. His father in the front room explaining a holding call to two schools that can’t hear him. His grandmother asleep in her chair by the window. Rosie under the table with a crab.
“That’s the house,” she says. “That’s what I wanted.”
Tomorrow is the font: Our Lady of the Holy Rosary, the afternoon. “Father scheduled it during the game. Daddy has written to the Archbishop.” And the gown. She tells it to him from the bed, low.

“It’s Grandmère’s. She made it for Luc, in 1985. Every stitch — there’s a lily on the hem you can only see if you know it’s there. Every one of us wore it. The twins had to take turns at the font, and Josie went first, because she was louder.” The cricket. “It was in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge for the storm. That’s why we have it. It’s the only thing Grandmère made that we still have. It smells like the chest. I ironed it myself tonight. I didn’t want anybody else to touch it.”
“How’d it come out?”

“Perfect. I used a pillowcase in between. Mama stood in the door and watched me like I was cutting the red wire.” And in the same breath as the ironing: “Luc asked Wes to stand in the back. He said he’d come to the house after. Not the church.”
She leaves it there. Jack looks at the dates on Nonna’s jars, and she goes on.
“Do you know what a godmother is, Jack? Actually. Not the dress.”
“You hold the candle.”

“You hold the candle, and you stand up in front of God and the whole parish and say that if Tess and Beau can’t, you will. That you’ll see she’s raised in it. Prayers at night, the sacraments, the hard parts — whatever they can’t do is yours.” The cricket. “Luc says it’s like co-signing on a car. Mama hit him with a spoon. But he’s not wrong. I sign tomorrow and I don’t get to un-sign. She’ll be forty and I’ll still be on the paper.”
“Jack. I need you to be the priest.”
“I’m not qualified.”

“You’re Catholic and you’re awake. In this house that’s a vocation.” The cricket. “Father is going to ask me the questions in front of God and Mama and everybody, and I have to answer them for her, because she can’t, and if I get a word wrong in front of Mémère I’ll have to move to Lafayette. She’ll be in the front pew with her lips going, half a word ahead of me, so she can catch me if I fall. I’ve never been responsible for anybody’s soul before. I can’t keep a fern alive.”

She has the booklet from the rectory; pages turn on her end. She reads him his part and then hers, so he’ll know where to stop, and he writes it on the back of Ma’s grocery pad with the pencil on the string.
*Do you reject Satan?* *I do.*
*And all his works?* *I do.*
*And all his empty promises?* *I do.*

Then the Creed, cut into its three questions — *Do you believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth?* — and the Son, born and crucified and risen, and the Spirit, the Church, the saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, the life everlasting, each of them with its *I do*. She whispers all of it from her childhood bed, and she’s surer on every one.
“Now you,” she says. “Ask me.”

choices.text: *Ask them straight, the way Father Dom would.*
choices.key: The night before the baptism Lena had you play the priest, and you asked her the promises straight.
response: He asks them straight, low, under the bulb, the way Father Dom would: no voice put on, just the questions. *Do you reject Satan?* *I do.* She answers every one, all the way down to the life everlasting.
“Again.”
He asks them again. She gets them all. The third time through, she doesn’t need the booklet, and he doesn’t need the grocery pad.

choices.key: The night before the baptism Lena had you play the priest, and you asked her the promises in Latin.
response: “*Abrenuntias Satanae?*”

“*Abrenuntio.*” Not a hitch. *Et omnibus operibus eius? Abrenuntio. Et omnibus pompis eius? Abrenuntio.* She knows the old rite cold, every *Credis* and every *Credo*, and gets to the end of it faster than he can find his place in his own church Latin.
She’s laughing by the end. “You say it like a Steelers fan.”
“Take that back.”
“Forty miles from Pittsburgh, Jack. It gets in the water.”

choices.key: The night before the baptism Lena had you play the priest, and you said the promises with her.
response: He asks the first, and she answers. He asks the second, and she answers. He asks the third — *And all his empty promises?* — and her *I do* comes, and under it, low, his.
When he starts the Creed she gets the first word of her answer wrong, and stops, and starts it over. She isn’t quite level through the first two questions. By the third she is. *I do.*

body: At 10:41 the cordless dies in the middle of her sentence — she is telling him about Josie’s First Communion, and the veil, and the cat — and there’s nothing on the line, and then the dial tone.

He stands under the bulb with the dial tone for half a minute. Then he reaches around the door and hangs the receiver on its hook, and it rings under his hand before it has settled, and he has it up again before his mother can get out of her chair in the front room.
“I’m standing in the hall with it plugged into the wall like a lamp,” Lena says. “Mama’s cordless is older than Remy, and Remy’s older than God.”

He finished *The Moviegoer* New Year’s night, after the game, and he didn’t read the end first. She wants to know that before anything. Her pencil goes all the way to the last page. He followed it for two days, *no* and *ha* and *oh, honey* down the middle of the book, and at the very end, under the children in the car, in a harder pencil than the rest: *wrong*.
“So you agree with me,” he says.
“About what? You haven’t said anything yet.”

“It’s a surrender. He spends the book looking — for God, for the thing behind the thing, whatever he calls it that week — and then it’s Ash Wednesday and he marries Kate and signs up for medical school and the looking stops. And the book wants me to call that grace. It’s a guy who got tired and took the job.”
“That’s what she said. The girl with the pencil. Word for word, and she was very proud of herself.” A door on her end. “I was seventeen. I argue with her too.”
“So argue.”

“He doesn’t stop looking, Jack. He stops looking *by himself*.” She’s going now, the long sentence building to its verdict. “The looking by himself was the sickness. It’s right there at the front, Kierkegaard — the despair that doesn’t know it’s despair. A man alone in a movie house in Gentilly looking for God is a man who has decided God is something you find on your own, like a parking space. And at the end he’s got Kate, and he’s got those children asking him about their brother, and he *answers* them. A man who quit doesn’t answer children.”

“Then where’s God in it? He looks for Him the whole book, and at the end he won’t say the word. Grace is supposed to *happen* to you. Paul on the road. Augustine in the garden — *take and read*. It knocks you down in the dirt. It doesn’t sign you up for medical school.”

“Grace perfects nature, Costigan. It doesn’t cancel it. You keep wanting God to show up like a fire truck.” Down the hall a door, and her voice drops back to the hall’s size. “Most people He gets the regular way. A wife. A job. Some children who need somebody to answer them. Percy didn’t put God in a speech. He put Him in the car.”
“That’s Ohio talk. Get a job, get married, don’t make a fuss.”
“That’s *Thomas* talk, and you know it. You only like the dirt because you’ve never had to live in it after.”
“And the grace part?”
“Is the part where he lets them in the car.”
“You wrote *wrong* in pencil, though.”
“I write everything in pencil, Costigan. I’m Catholic. I expect to be corrected.”
Out on the kitchen table, through the inch of door, the book lies shut by his milk with her *wrong* in it.
“My brother asked me something at Christmas,” he says. “I can’t answer it yet.”
“The truck?”
“Before that.”

She doesn’t ask what. “Then don’t answer it till you can.” The cordless chirps in the hall, plugged in or not. “Some things you have to grow into. Lucille’s going to be swimming in that gown tomorrow, and it’s still hers.”

They go on to things that don’t matter, which matter. He tells her about Nonna’s lentils, a spoon each for the money, and Rosie stacking hers into quarters on the rim of the bowl. “For *money*? We do cabbage. Y’all are smaller about it.” And about Rosie: “That child is going to run the Vatican Bank, and it’ll be the first time the books balance.” She has taken the cordless back to bed — “It’s had its rest” — and it chirps at her every few minutes, and she ignores it like a little brother. She’s in the middle of what Remy did on the levee at midnight, not with anything that lights, Mama’s rule held, with something worse, when she says, lightly, in the same breath:
“How’s California?”

choices.key: When Lena asked how California was, you told her: three hours behind.
response: “Three hours behind.”
“It always was,” she says, and goes on to the rest of Remy.

choices.key: When Lena asked how California was, you told her: far away.
response: “Far away.”
“Good,” she says, and goes on to the rest of Remy.

choices.key: When Lena asked how California was, you told her you weren’t thinking about California tonight.
response: “I’m not thinking about California tonight.”
It’s true tonight. It’s true in this pantry with the cord through the door.
“Okay,” she says, softer after it, and goes on to the rest of Remy.

choices.text: “There’s nothing in California, Lena. It’s a beach.”
choices.key: When Lena asked how California was, you told her there was nothing there but a beach.
response: “There’s nothing in California, Lena. It’s a beach.”
“Tell that to the beach,” she says, and goes on to the rest of Remy, and believes him.

body: At 11:25 the cordless chirps three times fast and gives up for good. This time when he hangs up it takes a minute, and when the wall rings again the line is nearer, cleaner, her own phone.
“Mama’s cordless,” Lena says, “has given its life for the Church.”

The house has gone up while they talked. The game is off in the front room; Ma said goodnight through the pantry door and he said it back with his hand over the mouthpiece. He comes out and sits down on the kitchen floor with his back against the cabinet under the sink, as far as the cord will reach, and puts his legs out on the linoleum. The light over the stove is the only one on. Under the floor the furnace is running; he can feel it come up through the tiles.

Nothing that matters, for most of an hour. The 8-Ball is on her nightstand, and she shakes it once about tomorrow and reads it to him: *You may rely on it.* “I shook it one time. I’m a godmother, Costigan. I don’t cheat.” Remy, somewhere in her house, singing along to something, wrong. Whether godmothers get a pew. (“The front one. Daddy already measured it.”) Whether a godmother can wear red. Mémère says no. Lena is wearing white anyway. “Mémère says that’s showing off. I said it’s the *Church’s* color, Mémère, take it up with the Pope.” Lucille is at Tess and Beau’s tonight; tomorrow she gets handed over at the church door, gown and all. “She won’t remember one minute of it,” Lena says. “That’s what the paper’s for. Everybody else remembers it for her.”
“Where are you now?”
“The kitchen floor.”

“Jack Costigan, get up off that floor, you’ll catch your death.” Her mother’s exact sentence, he’d bet the truck on it. He doesn’t get up. He tells her the furnace is under him and the stove light is on and the whole house is asleep except the refrigerator, and she says that’s the saddest thing she ever heard and the nicest, and to stay there, then, if he’s going to be stubborn.
A little before midnight she yawns in the middle of a word and denies it.
“I have to sleep. I have somebody’s soul at two o’clock.” A rustle, the sheet or the horse. “Come back, Youngstown.”
“I’m coming back.”
“Good. Goodnight, Jack.”

Two hours on his mother’s phone, and she never once said Julian’s name. Julian is staying in that house — in Remy’s room, the last Jack heard, with his shoes lined up under the bed. Jack listened for it from the first word.
The cord lies across the linoleum from the wall to his hand.

body: The Browns kick off in Cleveland at one with the colored lights still up on the pegboard till Wednesday, and the space heater going, and the Stroh’s fridge shut. Frank has the bucket. Jack has the duct-taped chair. The radio on the bench has the Jaguars, who came a long way to do this, Frank says, and the RAZR is face up on Jack’s knee, because somewhere in the middle of the Saints game a priest in New Orleans has a baby to baptize.

body: He reads that one to his father, who is leaning in toward the radio with his elbows on his knees and his hands hanging. Frank thinks about it through a Jacksonville punt. “Good timing,” he says.
At the next commercial: “What’s the baby’s name.”
“Lucille.”
Frank nods at the radio. “That’s a name.” A man in Parma wants to sell them a furnace. “The Saints girl’s the godmother.”
“Yeah.”
“Huh,” Frank says, and Cleveland comes back on, and that’s all he has on the subject.
At five after four the man in Cleveland gives it to them: Browns 23, Jaguars 17. Frank sits back on the bucket with his hands on his knees.
“Four straight.”

body: At twenty past nine the garage is down to the heater and the colored lights, and the radio is unplugged, and the supper plates are soaking inside. He dials. It’s twenty past eight on Dupre Street, and she picks up in a kitchen: a refrigerator door, foil coming off a roll, Mémère in French in the next room.

“She wore it,” Lena says, before hello. “Every lily. I signed the paper, in pen.” “She spit up on Father’s stole at the Creed and he said it was the most sincere profession of faith he’d had all year.” The foil. “Daddy listened to the whole fourth quarter in the vestibule with the radio to his ear like a man waiting on a kidney. Then he came back in and held her and cried. I don’t know which part he was crying about. He doesn’t either.”
“Okay. Your turn.”

body.text: She asks before he can get a word in. “Did he get out?”
“He turned it off himself.”
“He asked me was I going to sit there all day.”
“Ma drove. He got out first.”
“He turned the key.”
“He went in,” Jack says. “Last Sunday too.”
“Last *Sunday*? You didn’t tell me.”
“I left him out.”
“Danny was laughing at my face. It took the whole call.”
“It was long.”
“Tell me now.”

choices.text: *Tell her all of it — the lot, the room, “They’ll win.”*
response: He tells her all of it, from the lot, and she lets him get to the end with Dupre Street going on behind her, the foil and the refrigerator and somebody laughing in the den.

response.text: The key, his father turning it himself, and the radio dying in the middle of a man’s sentence.
The mirror, and his father’s eyes in it: *You gonna sit there all day?*
Ma at the curb, taking the keys out of his father’s hand without a word.
The key turning, and nobody saying anything about it.

response: The paper star over the microwave. Danny standing up. *They’ll win.* Four straight.
“Tell your daddy a godmother said good.”

Her end has filled up with leftovers — every aunt in the parish brought a pan — and she has to go wrap a hundred things in foil before Mama starts crying at the refrigerator. “Night, Jack.” He sits on under the colored lights with the phone shut on his knee.

“Good,” she says. “Then he’s further than I thought.” The foil stops. “You know what that means? Next time you don’t have to be there. You’ll be in California and he’ll go anyway.” The foil starts again. “Tell your daddy a godmother said so.”

“Tell him we’ll take one off his hands in February. Y’all can have the winning streak. We’ll take the game that counts. Did he say anything? In the room?” “He told Danny somebody’d been to Bethlehem.” “Lord.” And she’s off into the Saints, the bye week, the Dome, whether Brees’s shoulder is a state secret, and the call goes on to nothing much.

body: Monday he called from the garage at ten, with the radio off. Tuesday from the Giant Eagle lot with Ma’s list on the dash and the engine running for the heater. Tonight it’s the front porch, in the Carhartt, with the lights down off the house and Glenwood dark end to end except for the streetlights and the inflatable snowman across the street, which hasn’t heard. He dials, and she picks up on the first ring. He has called her every night since Sunday. He listens to every word she says for where she is.
Tonight is Twelfth Night, and she has news.
“It’s Carnival now,” Lena says. “Out here too.”

At dusk the Phunny Phorty Phellows rode the St. Charles streetcar in their masks, the way they do every Twelfth Night, throwing from the back, and one of them threw a strand of beads at Mémère on the neutral ground, and Mémère threw it back at him. “She told him she isn’t that kind of woman and it isn’t Mardi Gras yet. He caught it. He bowed to her off the back of a streetcar.”
And the first king cake, after supper, purple and green and gold sugar all over Mama’s good tablecloth — and she got the baby.

“It was in my second bite. A little plastic baby, about the size of a peanut, and I didn’t swallow it, which is how you know God loves me. Remy wanted it ruled a foul because I looked. I didn’t look. I *felt*.”
“Which means the next one’s mine,” she says. “I’m bringing it on the plane. On my lap. Laney says that’s a federal crime.”
“Is it?”
“It’s a *pastry*, Jack. It’s a Catholic pastry. Let them try.”

He tells her the lights came down today, and the house looks like it got caught without its coat. “We don’t take ours down,” she says. “We change the colors. Purple, green and gold by Sunday. Mémère says you don’t put away a party, you hand it to the next one.”
Down the block a storm door opens, and a man carries a dead tree out to the curb by its trunk and lays it down on the snowbank with the others.

The garage looks bigger with the lights down. The pegboard is bare except for the painted shapes of the tools that live on it, and the Stroh’s fridge hums against the back wall with ginger ale in it, and the space heater has the near half of the room to itself. His duffel is already behind the seat of the truck for the morning. It’s half past nine on Dupre Street. He dials.

Her house is all suitcases. “Everybody’s flying somewhere. Mémère goes back to Breaux Bridge Sunday, the twins go back to school Monday, I’m Sunday at noon, and Josie has written an agenda for the airport. It has times on it. It has a column for *notes*.” A zipper, close by. “Mémère is packing me a jar of something for the dormitory. I asked what. She said *for the dormitory*. It’s not going to get through security. It’s not going to get through *Mama*.”

The king cake is in its box on the kitchen table, and nobody is allowed to look at it. “If the TSA wands my king cake I’m going to make a scene, Jack, and it’s going to be a Broussard scene. They’ll have to call the Coast Guard.”

Tess brought Lucille for supper and took her home asleep. “At the table she reached up and got my medal in her fist — just took it — and wouldn’t let go. Tess had to open her fingers one at a time. She has a grip like Daddy. Mémère crossed herself and said she’d known it all along, I don’t know what. She’s going to be a terror and I’m going to let her.”

body.text: “I never told you. I ate your oyster. I ate two.”

body: “Is it snowing?” “It’s always snowing.” “I’ve seen snow twice in my life, Jack, and once it was hail.” He tells her his father is driving him to Pittsburgh in the morning, because Pittsburgh is cheaper, and she says only Ohio would drive to another state to leave it.

She wants to know what he did all day. Packed. Ma ironed his shirts, all four, and stacked them on Danny’s bed like the bed was going too. Rosie is making him a drawing for the door and has told him it’s a secret and that it’s a plane. “Then you act surprised,” Lena says. “Practice your face tonight. You have a terrible surprised face. I’ve seen it.”

She wants to know what he’s bringing back. He tells her: the Carhartt, a Tupperware of pizzelles Ma has packed in wax paper like they’re going to the moon, and a book he finished. She’s bringing the Greene for the plane, the one on Hale’s list. She has read it twice. “I hate her. I love her and I hate what she does. Hale’s going to make us fight about it in front of everybody, you know he is.” Remy goes back to Baton Rouge in the morning with a laundry bag the size of a person. Luc is on nights. The Saints play next Saturday, whoever wins Sunday, and her daddy is already sick to his stomach about both of them. “I’m watching it in the Fishbowl,” she says, “and y’all are going to be quiet, and nobody is going to say anything to me till it’s over.”
Then there’s a scuffle on her end, and a different voice altogether, old and French and much too close to the phone.
“*C’est le garçon d’Ohio?* You eating up there?”
“Yes, ma’am.”

“*Menteur.*” And then, as if it settles something: “When you come to New Orleans, you come to this house first.” And she’s gone, and it’s Lena again: “Sweet suffering Saint Sebastian. I’m sorry. She does that.”
She lands Sunday at four. Laney’s getting her; Kevin’s driving, because Theo won’t let Laney touch his car. “Monday is Hale,” she says. “He’s got us at opposite ends.”
“For the safety of the others.”
“I’m taking the end by the window.”
“Julian gets back Sunday too,” she says. “Late.”
It’s the first time she’s said his name in a week.
“Yeah?”
“I’m going to see him Monday.”
Jack looks at the bare pegboard.
“I haven’t been fair to him, Jack. I’ve known it a while. I’m going to fix it.”

It’s what she has always done. Where Julian is, when he lands, when he calls at ten his time — since September she has kept him posted, like a girl reading him the weather in a town he’ll never see. And under it, after a week of him dialing this number every night, he hears something being shut, gently, the way you’d shut a door on somebody asleep. She’s going home to make it right with Julian. She’s telling him so he’ll stop calling.
